subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Mentor's note, hostel year group. On Monday Nandini came to me shaken. A cruel post about a first-year had sat in the 120-member hostel chat for six hours, with forty reactions and no reports. Nandini said, "I saw it in the morning and thought somebody must have flagged it already." The sender, Ojas, had not been named by anyone. Nandini realised each reader had thought the same. We reported it to the warden together that hour, and the warden spoke with the first-year and the sender before evening. I told Nandini that assuming someone else has reported is very common, and that being the one who does is useful, not silly. — Meena Ma'am

qa.q: How many members were in the hostel chat?
What was Nandini feeling when coming to the mentor on Monday?
qa.a: Nandini was shaken and guilty, having assumed someone else would report the post; realising everyone had thought the same made the assumption feel heavy.

qa.q: What turning point did Nandini and the mentor take that hour?
qa.a: They reported the post to the warden together straight away, and the warden spoke with the first-year and the sender before evening.

qa.q: What might the first-year have been going through during the six hours the post stayed in the chat?
qa.a: The first-year may have felt exposed and humiliated with no sign anyone cared, as forty people reacted and nobody reported.

grounding: A student sees a cruel post in a big group chat and assumes someone else will report it, since the bigger the group the smaller each person's felt duty.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Saturday. Somebody put a photo of Vandana with a cruel caption in the big class chat, ninety people. My thumb hovered over the report button. Then I thought: with ninety of us, surely someone has already done it. I put the phone down and made tea. An hour later the photo was still there and Vandana had left the chat. That was when I felt sick. I hit report, then messaged Vandana: "I saw it. I am sorry I waited. Do you want to tell our class teacher together?" She wrote back "ok". We called the teacher that evening. The teacher answered, asked for screenshots, and got the post taken down before night. — Anirban

qa.q: How many people were in the class chat?
qa.a: The class chat had ninety people.

qa.q: Why did Anirban put the phone down without reporting the photo?
qa.a: Anirban assumed that with ninety people someone else must have reported it, so the felt duty was small; the sick feeling came later when Vandana left the chat.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make once the sick feeling arrived?
qa.a: Anirban reported the photo, apologised to Vandana and offered to call the class teacher together, which turned regret into action.

qa.q: What might Vandana have felt when leaving the chat and later reading Anirban's message?
qa.a: Vandana was probably hurt and humiliated on leaving, and may have felt some comfort at the message, though the plain "ok" shows caution.

grounding: A student sees a cruel post in a big group chat and assumes someone else will report it, then acts once the harm is clear.
